profile.summary: Esther narrates as a Jew of the diaspora, inserted in the Persian court, was used to save his people in the midst of a deadly crisis. The book presents a plot marked by twists, honor and humiliation, in which Esther's courage, Mordecai's fidelity and God's providential action, although not explicitly named in the text, lead the liberation of the Jews. The work does not inform authorship or date clearly; ancient traditions associated it with Esdras or Mordecai, but the most likely is a composition between the end of Xerxes' reign and the Persian conquest by Alexander, reflecting an authentic Persian context.
profile.setting: The setting is the Persian empire during the reign of Xerxes, between 486 and 465 BC, when Persian power was at its peak, with wealth concentrated in the capital Susa and grand palace projects. The backdrop includes the return of part of the Jews to Judea in previous generation, while many remained scattered throughout Persia, including the Esther's family. The narrative places a Jew living within the court of a pagan king, facing the tension between loyalty to his people and the demand to serve in a hostile environment.

structure.label: The Fall of Vasti and the choice of Esther
structure.description: The king promotes a banquet, Vasti refuses to display himself before the Persian leaders, and this leads to his deposition; then Esther is chosen as a new queen.

structure.label: Haman's rise and the decree against Jews
structure.description: Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, which provokes the revenge of the high officer and his conspiracy to exterminate the Jews of the empire.

structure.label: Fasting, risk and first approach to the king
structure.description: The Jewish community unites in prayer and Esther exposes himself to danger by entering without being called before the king and inviting him and Haman to a banquet.

structure.label: The reversal of Haman's honor and humiliation
structure.description: The king discovers that Mordecai was never rewarded for denouncing the conspiracy against his life, and Haman is forced to honor him; then, at the banquet, Esther reveals the plan against his people.

structure.label: The condemnation of Haman
structure.description: Haman's plot is undone, and he is killed in the very force he had prepared for Mordecai.

structure.label: Defense of the people and victory of the Jews
structure.description: The king authorizes the Jews to defend themselves; they triumph over their enemies, Haman is judged with severity, Mordecai is promoted, and there is celebration for liberation.

structure.label: Institution of the feast of Purim
structure.description: The narrative concludes with the collective memory of God's surrender through the annual celebration of the victory of the Jewish people.

themes: Divine Providence acting behind the scenes of history
Courage and risk for God's people
Irenonic reversal: the evil plot returns on the author himself
Identity and fidelity in the context of exile and pagan power
Prayer, fasting and responsible action of the community
readingKeys: Observe the narrative twists: the book works a lot with inversions of honor, power and destiny.
Notice how the explicit absence of God's name does not mean absence of his performance; the whole plot suggests providential direction.
Follow the progression of the risk of Esther: from the initial silence to public courage before the king.
Read Mordecai and Haman in contrast: one promotes the good of the people; the other, self-glorification and revenge.
profile.cautions: The authorship and date of the book are not informed in the biblical text and remain discussed; ancient traditions have proposed different names, but the evidence suggests composition in Persian period or shortly after. There are also later additions in Greek and Latin traditions that do not belong to the Hebrew text received and should not be confused with the biblical book in its canonical form.

dossier.narratedEra: The book is set in the Persian empire under Xerxes/Ahasuerus, in the period of 486-465 BC, when Susa functions as winter capital and Persian power is at its peak. The backdrop includes an earlier generation of return to Judah in 538 BC, but history accompanies Jews who remained in the Persian diaspora.
dossier.compositionEra: The date of composition is not indicated in the biblical text. The given notes state that the book was probably written between 460 BC and 331 BC, based on the presence of many Persian terms and the absence of Greek influence. The traditional authorship is attributed in an ancient way to Ezra by some church parents, and Mordecai by Clement of Alexandria; Matthew Henry considers Mordecai the author probable, but this remains inference, not explicit given from the book.

politics.title: Persian Empire at the height under Xerxes
politics.detail: Xerxes rules a vast empire, with 127 provinces going from India to Ethiopia; the notes place him in the apogee of Persian power, with Susa as the winter capital and Persepolis as the new luxurious palatial center. This scales the crisis: the threat against Jews is not local, but imperial.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that salvation comes in a scenario of superpower, which makes the reversal of events even more striking.

politics.title: Real power, irrevocable decrees and legal advice
politics.detail: The king consults wise and issues written decrees that cannot be revoked. The notes highlight that this Persian legal practice makes the political decision apparently irreversible, including in the case of Vasti and then in the conflict with the Jews.
politics.readingImpact: The plot gains legal tension: Esther's liberation depends on a change that, humanly, seems impossible.

politics.title: Haman as high officer and the dispute with Mordecai
politics.detail: Haman is presented as the highest official of Xerxes. Mordecai's refusal to bow to him turns a personal rivalry into an imperial plan of extermination against all Jews.
politics.readingImpact: The opposition between a proud officer and a loyal Jew shows how a courtly honor conflict can turn national threat.

politics.title: Real Authorization for Jewish Defense
politics.detail: After Esther's revelation, Xerxes allows the Jews to defend themselves from their enemies. The notes treat this as a decisive political turning within the empire.
politics.readingImpact: Reading begins to emphasize not only deliverance, but also political legitimacy for resistance and self-protection.

politics.title: Promotion of Mordecai and imperial administration
politics.detail: Mordecai ends up to a high position of government, described in the notes as a kind of prime minister. This suggests Jewish insertion in the Persian administrative apparatus, not just marginal survival.
politics.readingImpact: The end shows that providence includes public recognition and political influence, not just physical preservation.

customs.title: Real Banquets and Public Commitment
customs.detail: The first chapter describes an extended 180-day party for leaders, followed by another banquet for people from all social levels. The notes explain that this exhibited imperial wealth, power and pomp; the consumption of wine is portrayed without restriction.
customs.readingImpact: The environment of excess helps to understand why impulsive decisions and public humiliations happen so easily.

customs.title: Cutting label and risk of entering into the king's presence
customs.detail: Esther enters only before the king when he extends to him the golden scepter; without invitation, the entrance could mean death. Notes also note that she requests with deference and follows protocol when she postpones her request.
customs.readingImpact: Esther's gesture is not only courageous; it is an act highly regulated by the real etiquette, which makes his initiative look even more risky.

customs.title: Palace, harem and eunuchs
customs.detail: The notes explain that eunuchs served in frequent contact with the women of the real harem. This helps to situate the feminine sphere of the palace and the distance between the queen and the male public space.
customs.readingImpact: Esther's story is more concrete: it acts within a closed, hierarchical and controlled palatial system.

customs.title: Fasting for community in times of crisis
customs.detail: Before Esther acting, the Jewish community fasts; Matthew Henry emphasizes that there were Jews scattered in the provinces and that their preservation was also the object of providence. This appears as collective support for the Queen's intervention.
customs.readingImpact: Evangelical reading sees here spiritual solidarity: Esther's action is not isolated, but surrounded by community sustenance.

customs.title: Stake execution and public exhibition
customs.detail: Haman arranges a high stake for Mordecai. Notes treat this as a common means of execution and suggest that the height served for public display and humiliation.
customs.readingImpact: The instrument thought for terror becomes a symbol of reversal: the planned violence against Mordecai ends up falling on Haman.

customs.title: Purim as Jewish festive memory
customs.detail: The liberation leads to the first Purim Festival, and Matthew Henry connects this to Mordecai's letters for the event to be remembered. The book ends, thus, shaping a custom of community celebration.
customs.readingImpact: The story does not end in the immediate deliverance; it becomes a calendar of religious and national memory.

language.title: Persian names and transliteration
language.detail: The notes note that Xerxes is the Greek form of the Persian Xshayarshan, while the Hebrew brings akhashwerosh/Ahasuerus. This confirms the Persian fit of the book without resorting to fanciful reading.
language.readingImpact: The form of the names reinforces the imperial setting and helps the reader to perceive the text as narrating events in a real Persian court.

language.title: Decree in various languages and writings
language.detail: The decree is published in each region in its own writing and language. The note highlights the intention to make order intelligible throughout the empire.
language.readingImpact: This shows the Persian administrative breadth and the dispersion of Jews amidst many peoples and languages.

language.title: Idiomatic royalgia: 'up to half the kingdom'
language.detail: When the king says he would grant 'up to half the kingdom', the note explains that it is a conventional language of generosity, not unlimited literal promise.
language.readingImpact: Esr's request should be read within the rhetorical label of the cut, which makes the scene more subtle and politically charged.

language.title: Irony and narrative reversal
language.detail: The notes insist that the book works for a chain of providences and ironies: the king's banquet, the pride of Haman, the strategic delay of Esther and the unexpected honor of Mordecai. Matthew Henry reads the book as a narrative whose end clarifies the beginning.
language.readingImpact: The reader must accompany the reversals as theological and literary structure, not just as historical coincidences.

language.title: Vast name and possible title nuance
language.detail: The note says Vasti may mean 'the best, desired, beloved', suggesting that it is perhaps an honorary title and not a proper name. This observation is presented with caution.
language.readingImpact: This prevents hasty readings about the queen and shows that some onomlastic details of the text are discussed, not absolute.

language.title: The Book Without God's Name
language.detail: Both Tyndale and Matthew Henry observe that God's name does not appear in the Hebrew text, but that divine action is perceived in the providence that directs minimal events. Henry contrasts this with later additions, where God is explicitly mentioned.
language.readingImpact: The absence of the divine name shifts reading to hidden providence: God acts without being appointed.

timeline.title: 538 BC: partial return of Babylonian exile
timeline.detail: The notes recall that about 50,000 people returned to Judah in a previous generation, in 538 BC, according to Ezra. Esther, however, belongs to the family of those who remained in Babylon/Persia.
timeline.readingImpact: The book gains contrast between those who returned to the land and the Jews still dispersed; providence reaches both.

timeline.title: 486-465 BC: reign of Xerxes
timeline.detail: This is the explicit chronological picture given to the government of Xerxes, within which the entire main narrative unfolds.
timeline.readingImpact: The story should be read as an episode of the classical Persian period, not as a vague tradition without historical anchorage.

timeline.title: After Xerxes: Artaxerxes I
timeline.detail: The notes identify Artaxerxes I as the son of Xerxes who reigned after him, offering a mooring point for the Persian dynastic sequence.
timeline.readingImpact: This given helps the reader to situate the narrative within a real transition of reign in the empire.

timeline.title: 460-331 BC: Probable composition window
timeline.detail: The appropriation proposed in the notes ranges from the end of Xerxes' reign until before the conquest of Alexander the Great in 331 BC. The basis is linguistic and historical, not an internal date of the book.
timeline.readingImpact: This guides the reading of the book as a text produced within the Persian world, probably not long after the narrated events.

timeline.title: Institution of Purim after liberation
timeline.detail: After the defeat of Haman's plan, the Jews established the celebration of Purim as the annual memory of deliverance. Matthew Henry associates this with Mordecai's letters to preserve the memory of the event.
timeline.readingImpact: The historical outcome becomes a liturgical and community calendar, linking memory and identity.

investigation: To compare the probable dating (460-331 BC) with the absence of explicit date in the text and with the tradition of authorship attributed to Ezra or Mordecai.
Observe how notes use authentic Persian customs, especially decree, banquet, court etiquette and imperial administration, to support historical reading.
Read the role of Haman, Mordecai and Esther as a court dispute that extends to imperial politics.
To see how silence about God's name works literally with the emphasis on providence.
Follow the link between the narrative and the origin of Purim, without mixing the Hebrew text with later additions.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes and therefore is selective: it does not try to reconstruct everything that is historically known about the Persian period. Some statements are explicitly interpretative, such as the probable authorship, the composition window and the reading of the providence as the book's axis. The historicity of certain elements is recognized in the notes as debated, and the information about the additions to the book indicates that Targum, Midrash, Septuagint, Vulgate and Josephus include later material that does not belong to the Hebrew text and does not always agree with it. No external data have been added to fill gaps.
